q: Is Lumetri going away now that there's a node grader?
a: Neither replaces the other: Lumetri Color (one panel of sliders, wheels and curves, stored as an effect on the clip) is there for Premiere habits, the node grader for Resolve habits. Both are built from the same small colour operations (lift / gamma / gain, curves, HSL key, saturation, LUT, colour space transform), so the same setting gives the same picture in either.

q: Which is applied first, the effects or the grade?
a: Every clip runs: input transform, your grade nodes, the clip's effects (Lumetri is one of them), output transform. So a node grade and Lumetri are both applied, nodes first; Lumetri sees the picture the nodes made. Bypass turns the node grade off and leaves Lumetri on; Lumetri has its own fx switch in its header.

q: How does Lumetri's white balance eyedropper work?
a: In Basic Correction ▸ Color click WB Selector, then click or drag on something grey or white in the Program monitor: Temperature and Tint are set so it becomes neutral, in one undo step (`lumetri.wb.pick`). Auto balance does it from the frame's greys (`lumetri.wb.auto`). It samples after the Input LUT, refuses clipped, too dark or too colourful spots, and removes keyframes from Temperature / Tint.

q: In Premiere I'd use the Lumetri Color panel. Is it the same here?
a: Yes: it follows Premiere's sections and names, so Premiere habits carry over. The one difference: the fork's node grader runs before Lumetri on each clip; if you never open it, nothing changes.

q: What's the benefit of one job per node?
a: One job per node (balance, exposure, contrast, a look) lets you switch any step off, see what each did, and copy only the steps you want to other clips. Today the chain is serial: node 1 feeds node 2 feeds node 3, and the grade belongs to the clip.

q: Are nodes connected in series or in parallel today?

q: What does the Nodes panel show?

Click a box to select it, double-click it to disable or enable it.

q: What's the id of a node box?

q: How do I add a serial node?
a: 1. Select a clip and press Add Node in Primaries (or + Serial in Nodes): box 01. 2. + Serial adds 02 after it, again for 03. 3. Click 01 and change Gain; click 03 and raise Grain strength. 4. Select 02 and press Disable: the picture changes by exactly that node's work; Enable restores it. 5. Bypass shows the clip ungraded; press again.

q: What happens to the nodes after one I delete?

q: In Resolve I'd label my nodes. How do I do that in Revolution?
a: Select the node and click Rename in the Nodes panel (or right-click ▸ Rename), type the name (Balance, Skin, Look) and press Enter. An empty name clears it and the node shows what it holds instead.

q: Explain the six nodes of the starter tree.
a: One common starting point, not the only right one: 1. Balance (Temperature / Tint, Offset) so later nodes work on a neutral picture. 2. Exposure (Gain, Gamma). 3. Contrast (Contrast and Pivot, or a gentle S curve). 4. Saturation, after contrast because steeper contrast also looks more saturated. 5. Secondaries (optional), after the primaries so they select colours that already look right. 6. Look, with film grain on the very last node. The input and output conversions around it are automatic.

Secondaries (optional), after the primaries so they select colours that already look right. 6. Look, with film grain on the very last node. The input and output conversions around it are automatic.

q: why are secondaries after the primaries there?
a: So the qualifier or window selects colours that already look right; selecting from the flat log picture is harder.

q: What's a simpler node tree for beginners?
a: A beginner tree is three nodes: Balance, Exposure / contrast, Look. Fewer nodes to keep track of, but you can't switch exposure and contrast off separately. Good for a first edit or when shots need little work; the six-step tree keeps one job per node so a client note touches one node.

q: What do I give up with only three nodes?
a: A beginner tree is three nodes: Balance, Exposure / contrast, Look. Fewer nodes to keep track of, but you can't switch exposure and contrast off separately. Good for a first edit or when shots need little work; the six-step tree keeps one job per node so a client note touches one node.

q: Is it ever OK to set exposure before balance?
a: Exposure first works when the cast is small, because casts are easier to judge at the right brightness; with a strong cast, balance first is safer. Highlight soft clip goes near the end, so it shapes the brightest values after everything else has pushed them and later nodes can't clip them again.

q: Where should highlight soft clip go in the tree?
a: Exposure first works when the cast is small, because casts are easier to judge at the right brightness; with a strong cast, balance first is safer. Highlight soft clip goes near the end, so it shapes the brightest values after everything else has pushed them and later nodes can't clip them again.

q: How do pro parallel trees work, and can I do that here?
a: In Resolve (and here after phase C2) pros run balance and exposure in series, then several secondaries side by side in a parallel node so each keys from the same picture, then a look node. Only serial nodes exist here today; a qualifier node placed after the primaries does the same job one at a time.

q: How should I treat Rec. 709 footage compared with log?
a: Footage matters: log (F-Log2) needs balance and exposure before any look; Rec. 709 footage often needs only a small balance and a look; noisy low-light shots benefit from noise reduction early. With mixed cameras, balance each camera's shots to match first, then share the look.

q: Is every node change undoable?

In the default Premiere workflow these commands have no shortcut.

q: Is there an outside node yet?
a: Yes. Right-click the node canvas and choose Add Outside Node (`grade.addOutside`): the new node works on everything outside the first node's selection.
